02

PRECISION

Measure what quantization changes.

Speed and accuracy share no single score here. The plots show both, with fixed axes across runtime selections on each device. Tiny AP changes remain tiny on the chart.

Speed: zero-based linear axis, whiskers show trial min–max. Accuracy: fixed −0.1 to 6.0 point axis, including small negative differences. The historical 1.0-point quality target is not treated as a validated acceptance boundary. AP uncertainty is unmeasured.

4,488 COCO evaluation images, disjoint from 512 calibration images. FP16/INT8 flags allow mixed execution; OpenVINO FP16 describes weight storage. Negative measured AP loss does not establish an improvement.

03

CAMERA LOAD

Show the latency curve.
Let the application set the limit.

Where did 100 ms and 15 FPS come from?

They were chosen study targets, fixed in the notebook before these runs. They were not derived from a customer requirement, traffic standard or validated counting task. The earlier pass/fail framing overstated their meaning. Results below are measurements, without those targets being treated as production acceptance criteria.

Six serving configurations, four camera loads, three repeats each. Rendering was off. Highlight a runtime to inspect its curve and repeat spread against the other recorded configurations.

X-axes: actual camera counts, linear scale. FPS: fixed zero-based 0–35 axis. Frame age: fixed 10–100,000 ms logarithmic axis; each major y-step is ×10. Points: medians of three repeats. Whiskers: highlighted runtime’s observed repeat min–max. No SLA line is assumed.

Compute-load replays of the original short recording, distinct from the Norway demo below. One decoder thread per camera; capacity-one queues drop the oldest decoded frame. Counting and traffic-domain accuracy are unvalidated. TensorRT FP16 was not in this serving matrix, so its camera capacity is unknown. Long sessions, independent views and network behavior remain untested.

04

PROFILING

Locate the work outside the detector.

TensorRT INT8, first recorded repeat. Stage p95 values share a fixed 0–120 ms scale. Decoder lag is a separate measure of lateness, not a stage duration.

Hollow markers: the measured one-camera reference

Interpretation

The measurements point to CPU work and decode pacing upstream of the detector. A bounded queue after decode does not remove lateness already accumulated before entry.

GPU decode, earlier resizing and skipping overdue source frames are proposed experiments, not completed optimizations.

All 72 recorded profiles ↓
05

METHOD & EVIDENCE

What the measurements establish.

Implemented

Detection, per-camera ByteTrack, crossing and zone telemetry, paced replay, bounded queues, profiling, isolated workers, resumable experiments and export/precision checks.

Comparison references

GPU throughput: eager PyTorch FP32, 95.92 FPS. CPU throughput: PyTorch FP32, 32.40 FPS. Accuracy: PyTorch CUDA FP32, 0.284270 COCO mAP and 0.332202 vehicle AP. Precision speed comparisons use the selected runtime’s FP32 result, stated beside the plot.

Limits

One host/session. One retained ONNX CUDA FP32 timing trial recorded a thermal flag. No AP confidence intervals or independent traffic labels. 640px and tuning were not completed. Per-image predictions are absent from the saved archive, so these downloads alone cannot reproduce AP.

Targets versus requirements

The historical 100 ms / 15 FPS timing targets and 1.0-point AP-loss target were experiment choices. No application-derived acceptance criteria were supplied. A deployment needs its own end-to-end latency and task-quality requirements.

Original report ↓Model results ↓Serving results ↓Paired comparisons ↓Artifact audit ↓

The original report retains historical target-based classifications for provenance; these are not validated capacity claims. The 2,753-check audit verifies identities and arithmetic, not independent reproduction. Exploratory paired log-ratio t-intervals assume approximately independent normal round log ratios and do not establish multi-day repeatability.
